title: Type 2 Diabetes Medications Beyond Metformin: Choose for the Patient's Cardiorenal and Hypoglycemia Risk
bottomLine: After or alongside metformin, medication choice should follow the patient's cardiovascular disease, heart failure, CKD, glycemic gap, hypoglycemia risk, weight goals, kidney function, adverse-effect profile, access and preference. Cardiorenal benefit can justify an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist even when A1C is already near target.
recognize: Diabetes Canada prioritizes therapies with established cardiorenal benefit for patients with relevant CV, HF or CKD risk.
Symptomatic severe hyperglycemia or metabolic decompensation is an insulin problem first rather than a slow oral-medication escalation problem.
differentiate: Sulfonylureas and insulin have greater hypoglycemia risk than most non-insulin alternatives.
DPP-4 inhibitor plus GLP-1 receptor agonist generally adds little clinical value and is not routine combination therapy.
assessment: Review A1C/glucose pattern, eGFR/albuminuria, ASCVD/HF, hypoglycemia, weight, GI history, pregnancy plans, costs/coverage and injection preference.
workup: Use renal/hepatic monitoring and contraindication screening appropriate to the selected agent; do not order broad tests unrelated to drug choice.
management: Select therapy according to cardiorenal indication and patient priorities, then reassess response/tolerability and de-intensify hypoglycemia-producing therapy when safer agents make it appropriate.
Use insulin promptly when catabolic symptoms or metabolic decompensation make non-insulin sequencing unsafe.
medicationSafety: SGLT2 inhibitors require sick-day/perioperative/euglycemic-DKA counselling; GLP-1 receptor agonists require GI/gallbladder/pancreatitis and contraindication review; secretagogues require active hypoglycemia prevention.
counselling: Explain when a medication is being chosen for heart/kidney protection rather than only for the A1C number.
followUp: Reassess glycemia, renal function when relevant, adverse effects, adherence/access and whether the medication still matches goals.
examTrap: Rejecting a cardiorenal-benefit drug because A1C is already controlled—or delaying insulin in a catabolic/decompensated presentation.
oneLinePearl: Choose diabetes drugs for the whole patient's outcomes, not only their A1C.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Pharmacologic Glycemic Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Adults — 2024 Update
Diabetes Canada CKD in Diabetes — 2025 Update

title: Insulin Initiation and Titration: Match Basal, Prandial, and Correction Insulin to the Glucose Pattern
bottomLine: Insulin titration is pattern-based. Basal insulin primarily targets fasting/background glucose, prandial insulin covers meals, and correction insulin addresses unexpected hyperglycemia; do not keep escalating basal insulin to treat isolated post-meal highs or recurrent daytime lows.
recognize: Basal insulin is often the simplest initial insulin strategy in type 2 diabetes when insulin is needed outside metabolic decompensation.
Type 1 diabetes requires ongoing basal insulin even when intake is poor; dose adjustment is different from complete omission.
differentiate: Fasting hyperglycemia suggests a basal/background problem; postprandial excursions suggest meal-related therapy.
Repeated nocturnal/fasting lows with daytime highs can represent over-basalization rather than inadequate total insulin.
assessment: Review SMBG/CGM patterns, meal timing, hypoglycemia, renal function, acute illness, steroid use, activity, injection technique and adherence.
workup: Use glucose/CGM patterns and A1C; evaluate ketosis/metabolic decompensation urgently when severe hyperglycemia is accompanied by illness or insulin deficiency.
management: Start and titrate using a validated diabetes plan with small pattern-driven dose changes and appropriate follow-up; add prandial therapy when fasting control is adequate but meal excursions remain problematic.
For acute illness/NPO, preserve necessary basal physiology while adjusting prandial/correction doses and monitoring more closely.
medicationSafety: Insulin can cause severe hypoglycemia and hypokalemia; CKD/frailty/irregular intake increase risk.
Use concentration/device checks and avoid dose transcription errors between insulin products.
redFlags: Insulin access interruption in type 1 diabetes
counselling: Teach hypoglycemia treatment, injection/device technique, sick-day rules and what to do when meals are missed.
followUp: Review patterns soon after initiation/titration and adjust the component causing the abnormal pattern rather than changing all doses at once.
examTrap: Continuing to raise basal insulin because the A1C is high even though fasting glucose is at target and the patient has nocturnal hypoglycemia.
oneLinePearl: Basal fixes background; prandial fixes meals; correction fixes unexpected excursions.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Clinical Practice Guidelines and glycemic-management tools

title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring: Read Time in Range, Lows, Variability, and the Daily Pattern
bottomLine: CGM interpretation is more than the average glucose. Confirm sufficient data quality, then review time below range first for safety, time in range, time above range, glucose variability and recurring overnight/meal/activity patterns before changing therapy.
recognize: CGM can reveal nocturnal or asymptomatic hypoglycemia that A1C hides.
Sensor lag and compression/technical artifacts can create readings that do not match symptoms or capillary glucose.
differentiate: A1C summarizes longer-term glycemia but does not show variability or timing; CGM provides pattern/time data.
A single dramatic CGM excursion should not override repeated pattern evidence or a discordant symptomatic capillary measurement.
assessment: Review wear time/data completeness, medication/insulin timing, meals, activity, sleep, symptoms, alarms and whether readings match the patient's experience.
workup: Use standardized CGM reports when available; confirm unexpected severe readings with capillary testing when device instructions/clinical circumstances require it.
management: Prioritize reducing clinically important hypoglycemia, then address persistent hyperglycemia and variability with targeted changes to the relevant therapy/behaviour.
Avoid changing multiple regimen components from one short or low-quality data segment.
medicationSafety: Automated insulin-delivery settings and CGM alarms should be adjusted with device-specific training; technology failure requires a backup glucose/insulin plan.
redFlags: CGM failure in insulin-dependent patient without backup plan
Sensor readings discordant with severe symptoms
counselling: Teach trend arrows and alarms as decision-support, not a command to repeatedly over-correct and create glucose cycling.
followUp: Compare patterns after a defined intervention and evaluate whether time in range and hypoglycemia improved.
examTrap: Titrating insulin from A1C alone despite CGM showing recurrent nocturnal hypoglycemia.
oneLinePearl: On CGM, protect against lows first—then interpret range, highs and variability by time of day.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Clinical Practice Guidelines — Monitoring Glycemic Control and Type 1 Diabetes resources

title: Thyroid Nodule: TSH, Ultrasound Risk, Then FNA Only When Indicated
bottomLine: A thyroid nodule is evaluated with clinical risk, TSH and structured ultrasound features; fine-needle aspiration depends on sonographic risk and size rather than palpability or patient anxiety alone. Suppressed TSH changes the pathway toward functional imaging rather than reflex FNA.
recognize: Rapid growth, hard/fixed mass, cervical nodes, persistent hoarseness, childhood neck radiation or strong thyroid-cancer history raise risk.
Most nodules are benign and many low-risk nodules can be monitored without biopsy.
differentiate: A hyperfunctioning nodule in a thyrotoxic patient follows a different workup from a euthyroid suspicious ultrasound nodule.
Routine thyroid ultrasound is not a screening test for nonspecific symptoms in patients without a palpable/risk finding.
assessment: Assess compressive/voice symptoms, radiation/family history, thyroid symptoms, pregnancy and cervical nodes.
workup: Obtain TSH and high-quality thyroid/neck ultrasound; use accepted ultrasound-risk categories and size thresholds for FNA.
If TSH is suppressed, use thyroid scintigraphy when indicated to evaluate autonomy rather than relying on ultrasound alone to determine thyrotoxicosis etiology.
management: Refer suspicious nodules/cytology and symptomatic compressive disease appropriately; surveil low-risk nodules at evidence-based intervals rather than repeated short-interval scans.
medicationSafety: Do not use routine levothyroxine suppression for benign nodules because harm can exceed benefit.
counselling: Explain that biopsy decisions are risk-pattern based and that monitoring a low-risk nodule is active evidence-based care.
followUp: Track cytology or surveillance imaging through a closed-loop plan.
examTrap: Biopsying every thyroid nodule or ordering ultrasound as the etiologic test for thyrotoxicosis with suppressed TSH.
oneLinePearl: Nodule decisions follow TSH plus ultrasound risk—not fear, palpability or one size rule.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Endocrinology and Metabolism recommendations

title: Adrenal Insufficiency: Recognize Crisis, Then Define Primary vs Central Disease
bottomLine: Suspected adrenal crisis is treated immediately with parenteral glucocorticoid and fluid resuscitation; confirmatory testing must not delay life-saving therapy. In stable disease, distinguish primary adrenal failure from central disease because mineralocorticoid involvement and the etiologic workup differ.
recognize: Weakness, weight loss, orthostasis, GI symptoms, hyponatremia and recurrent unexplained hypotension are clues; primary disease can add hyperkalemia, salt craving and hyperpigmentation.
Crisis can present with shock, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbance and altered mental status.
differentiate: Primary disease affects cortisol and often aldosterone; central disease usually preserves aldosterone.
Abrupt withdrawal after prolonged exogenous glucocorticoid exposure can cause secondary adrenal insufficiency.
assessment: Review steroid exposure, autoimmune history, pituitary disease, infection, cancer, medications, pregnancy and crisis triggers; assess hemodynamics and volume status.
workup: When stable, use appropriately timed cortisol/ACTH and stimulation testing according to endocrine guidance; obtain electrolytes/glucose and cause-directed testing.
In crisis, draw cortisol/ACTH if feasible before treatment but never delay glucocorticoid/resuscitation.
management: Treat crisis urgently with stress-dose glucocorticoid, isotonic fluids/glucose as needed and the precipitating cause.
Provide chronic glucocorticoid replacement and mineralocorticoid replacement when primary disease requires it, with endocrinology support.
medicationSafety: Never abruptly stop chronic systemic glucocorticoids when HPA suppression is plausible.
Patients need sick-day/stress-dose and emergency injectable steroid education.
counselling: Teach sick-day rules, medical identification, emergency injection and when illness requires emergency care.
followUp: Monitor symptoms, BP/electrolytes and replacement adequacy and investigate recurrent crises or uncertain etiology.
examTrap: Waiting for a stimulation test before giving glucocorticoid to a patient in suspected adrenal crisis.
oneLinePearl: Adrenal crisis is a treat-first endocrine emergency.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Endocrinology and Metabolism practice resources

title: Cushing Syndrome: Test the Discriminatory Phenotype, Exclude Exogenous Steroids First
bottomLine: Do not screen every patient with obesity, diabetes or hypertension for Cushing syndrome. Test when multiple progressive or discriminatory features create a meaningful pretest probability, and first identify exogenous glucocorticoid exposure from oral, injected, inhaled, topical or unregulated sources.
recognize: Easy bruising, proximal weakness, wide violaceous striae, facial plethora, unexplained osteoporosis and difficult hypertension/diabetes are more discriminatory than common obesity alone.
Children may present with weight gain plus growth deceleration.
differentiate: Depression, heavy alcohol use, severe obesity and physiologic stress can cause pseudo-Cushing biochemical patterns.
Exogenous steroid exposure is common and changes both diagnosis and safe taper planning.
assessment: Review all glucocorticoid exposure, trajectory of features, infections, fractures, thrombotic risk, menstrual/reproductive symptoms and medications that interfere with cortisol testing.
workup: Use validated first-line screening tests matched to the patient and repeat/confirm abnormal results before imaging/localizing a source.
Do not order random cortisol or proceed directly to pituitary/adrenal imaging as the initial diagnostic step.
management: Refer confirmed endogenous hypercortisolism for endocrine localization and definitive treatment; manage metabolic, bone, infection and thrombotic complications.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly stop chronic exogenous steroids when adrenal suppression is possible.
Cortisol-test interpretation can be altered by medications, shift work, pregnancy and severe illness.
counselling: Explain why common weight gain alone does not justify cortisol testing and why steroid history matters.
followUp: Confirm biochemical diagnosis before localization and monitor treatment-related adrenal insufficiency afterward.
examTrap: Ordering adrenal CT because an obese hypertensive patient 'looks Cushingoid' without establishing biochemical hypercortisolism or reviewing steroid exposure.
oneLinePearl: Cushing workup starts with phenotype and steroid exposure—biochemistry before imaging.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Endocrinology and Metabolism recommendations

title: Pheochromocytoma/Paraganglioma: Biochemical Confirmation Before Tumor Hunting
bottomLine: Suspect pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma in the right clinical/genetic context, then use recommended metanephrine-based biochemical testing before localization imaging. Plasma catecholamines are not the preferred first-line test, and beta blockade must not precede adequate alpha blockade in a confirmed/suspected catecholamine-secreting tumor requiring preoperative blockade.
recognize: Episodic or sustained hypertension with headache, palpitations, sweating, tremor or pallor can occur, but the classic triad is neither necessary nor specific.
Adrenal incidentaloma, hereditary syndrome or prior PPGL increases pretest probability.
differentiate: Panic, hyperthyroidism, medications/stimulants and withdrawal can mimic adrenergic episodes.
Routine plasma catecholamines are less appropriate than plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrine strategies for first-line biochemical assessment.
assessment: Review episodic symptoms, BP pattern, adrenal mass, family/genetic history, medications/interfering substances and pregnancy.
workup: Use plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines under appropriate collection conditions; interpret borderline results with pretest probability/interfering factors before imaging.
Localize with CT/MRI and genetic evaluation after biochemical evidence or in specialist-defined exceptions.
management: Refer confirmed/high-suspicion disease to endocrinology/surgical expertise; preoperative preparation uses alpha blockade/volume management under specialist protocol before beta blockade if required.
medicationSafety: Unopposed beta blockade can precipitate severe hypertension in catecholamine-secreting disease.
Several medications/stress states can cause false-positive biochemical results.
redFlags: Adrenal mass with severe adrenergic episodes
counselling: Explain why biochemical confirmation usually comes before imaging and why some medications/conditions affect the test.
followUp: Complete genetic/surveillance planning after confirmed disease because hereditary risk and recurrence can affect the patient and relatives.
examTrap: Ordering plasma catecholamines as the preferred first test or giving beta blockade before alpha blockade in a catecholamine-secreting tumor.
oneLinePearl: PPGL: metanephrines first, localization second, alpha before beta when blockade is needed.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Endocrinology and Medical Biochemistry recommendations

title: Pituitary Adenoma: Hormone Excess, Hormone Deficiency, or Mass Effect?
bottomLine: Pituitary lesions are assessed along three axes: hormone hypersecretion, pituitary hormone deficiency and mass effect. Do not interpret pituitary hormones like primary-gland disease—for example, a normal TSH can be inappropriate when free T4 is low—and urgent visual/neurologic symptoms require expedited assessment.
recognize: Headache, visual-field loss, galactorrhea/amenorrhea, acromegalic features, Cushing phenotype or hypopituitarism can reveal a pituitary lesion.
Pituitary apoplexy can present with sudden severe headache, visual/ocular motor deficits and adrenal insufficiency.
differentiate: Hyperprolactinemia can come from medications, pregnancy, hypothyroidism, stalk effect or prolactinoma.
Central hypothyroidism uses free T4 with an inappropriately low/normal TSH rather than a primary-thyroid TSH algorithm.
assessment: Assess headache/vision, menstrual/sexual function, growth/acromegaly features, cortisol/thyroid symptoms, medications, pregnancy and prior pituitary imaging.
workup: Use targeted pituitary hormone testing and dedicated MRI when indicated; perform formal visual-field testing for lesions near the optic chiasm.
Evaluate adrenal reserve before starting thyroid replacement if significant central hypopituitarism is possible.
management: Refer functioning macroadenomas, visual compromise, apoplexy or significant hypopituitarism to endocrine/neurosurgical care.
Treatment may be medical, surgical or surveillance depending on hormone type, size and symptoms.
medicationSafety: Starting levothyroxine before addressing unrecognized secondary adrenal insufficiency can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Dopamine agonist and other pituitary therapies require diagnosis-specific monitoring.
counselling: Explain why pituitary hormone interpretation differs from primary endocrine-gland testing and why visual symptoms need urgent attention.
followUp: Track hormone response, visual function and imaging according to lesion type and treatment.
examTrap: Calling thyroid function normal because TSH is normal despite a low free T4 and a pituitary mass.
oneLinePearl: Pituitary disease is three questions: excess, deficiency, and mass effect.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada endocrine laboratory principles
